chunks: Muhammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muhammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Wahb ibn Ḥafṣ, from Abū Baṣīr, who said:

I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) about a man who performed ẓihār with his wife. He said: 'If he had intercourse with her, then upon him is freeing a slave, or fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people. Otherwise, he is left [in the state of ẓihār] for three months. If he returns [to normal], and if not, he is held until he is asked: Do you have a need for your wife, or will you divorce her? If he returns [to normal], there is nothing upon him and she is his wife. If he divorces her once, then he has more right to take her back [in revocable divorce].'

key_terms.أَمْلَكُ بِرَجْعَتِهَا: Has more right to take her back

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for Zihar in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elaborates on the mechanics of ẓihār, specifically addressing the scenario where the husband abstains from intercourse for three months, triggering a judicial inquiry into his intent to reconcile or divorce. It highlights the Shia juristic view that if he chooses to remain married, the ẓihār is lifted without further expiation, whereas a single divorce allows for revocation (rajʿah), reflecting the procedural nuances in resolving marital estrangement. The text underscores the importance of the husband's active choice in resolving the status, distinguishing between mere abstention and formal separation.
